title: Proportional latency guarantees via credit-based batch arbitration and KV working-set reshaping
creator: Asha Patel
description: Problem: Continuous batching provides excellent throughput but can cause hard-to-predict tail latency for tenants/requests with strict SLOs due to variable KV cache residency and GPU memory pressure. We need a scheduler that enforces proportional latency guarantees across tenants and request classes while maximizing GPU utilization and avoiding expensive hard preempts. This ticket scopes a credit-based arbitration + working-set reshaping approach to: (1) bound p95/p99 latency for SLO-marked traffic; (2) reduce cross-tenant KV eviction churn; (3) adapt admission/batch composition under memory pressure to avoid OOMs and expensive model reloads.
acceptance_criteria: A production branch implements a credit-based batch arbitration algorithm and a complementary KV working-set reshaper behind a feature flag.
Measured on synthetic mixed workloads: p95 latency for SLO-tagged requests is within 1.2x of target under 95% of 10-minute windows at 80% GPU utilization.
KV cache churn (eviction+reloads/sec) decreases by >= 30% for mixed-tenant workloads compared to baseline preempt-on-demand policy.
No increase in OOM incidents in canary clusters during rollout; rollback plan documented and exercised.
Docs and a runbook are added: design doc, rollout checklist, dashboard links, and a postmortem template for regressions.
design_notes: High-level approach: assign each tenant/request-class a replenishing credit budget proportional to their SLO weight. Credits are consumed when requests get admitted into batches that risk increasing tail latency (long sequences, KV-miss heavy). When credits are exhausted, the scheduler defers admission or routes to a compatible lower-cost model variant.

KV working-set reshaper: periodically compute per-tenant KV residency scores (recency * request-weight) and apply low-impact pre-eviction of cold segments to lower memory pressure before admitting large batches. This is cooperative: the reshaper avoids evicting hot prefixes that would cause immediate reloads.

Soft vs hard preemption: prefer soft (batch admission throttling, delayed starts, targeted KV eviction) to reduce wasted compute. Hard preempt (token-level interruption) only used under imminent OOM or SLA-violating tail events.

Admission policy uses a multi-dimensional cost estimate: estimated extra GPU memory cost, expected added latency, and KV-miss probability. Credits reduce available budget for costly admissions so high-priority tenants maintain headroom.

Fairness model: proportional-share by SLO weight rather than equal shares. Allows paid tiers or enterprise customers to get higher credit rates while preserving minimum guarantees for low-tier tenants. Configurable floor and ceiling per tenant to prevent starvation or unbounded dominance.
Fallbacks: when capacity is constrained, route to lower-seq-length truncation, cached-response fallback, or a quantized model variant. All fallbacks recorded for quality monitoring.
implementation_plan: Phase 1 - Simulation and offline tuning: build a simulator (based on existing trace playback tools) to validate credit parameters and KV reshaper heuristics against representative traces.
Phase 2 - Scheduler prototype: implement credit accounting and admission hooks in the continuous batching scheduler behind a feature flag. Expose per-tenant credit config via config store.
Phase 3 - KV reshaper: instrument KV residency metrics and implement low-impact eviction passes. Wire into admission control to expose current memory headroom estimates.
Phase 4 - Canary rollout: enable on non-critical shard pool with synthetic mixed workloads and measure p95/p99, KV churn, and OOMs. Iterate thresholds.
Phase 5 - Gradual rollout and observability: expand to more pools, add dashboards and alert rules, and finalize runbook.
test_plan: Unit tests for credit accounting invariants (replenish, consume, leak-proof on restart).
Integration tests: admission hooks exercising combinations of KV pressure and batch sizes, asserting expected deferrals and fallback triggers.
Chaos tests: inject KV eviction bursts and simulate slow disk reads to verify soft-preempt logic avoids regression.
Performance tests: measure throughput and end-to-end latency under steady and bursty loads using the trace simulator.
Canary verification checks: p95/p99, KV eviction rate, OOM count, and fallback invocation rate.
rollout_plan: Stage 0: Run simulator and validate offline. (done before any cluster changes)
Stage 1: Deploy scheduler changes to canary pool with synthetic load for 48h. Abort on any OOM or p95 degradation >10%.
Stage 2: Enable KV reshaper in canary for 24h and validate KV churn reduction.
Stage 3: Expand to 10% of capacity with real traffic; monitor 72h. If signals stable, increase in 3x steps with 24–72h observation windows.
Rollback criteria: any sustained increase in OOM incidents, >20% regression in p99 for SLO-tagged traffic, or >2x increase in KV reload rate.
notes: Open question: optimal credit replenish cadence — continuous tiny replenishments vs pulsed bucket refill. Simulator will inform choice.

Open question: whether to account for KV reload cost in credits directly or treat it via separate memory headroom gate. Current plan uses both: credits throttle latency risk; headroom gate prevents OOMs.
Trade-off: more aggressive pre-eviction reduces immediate memory pressure but increases short-term reload IO; heuristic aims for steady-state reduction in reloads by evicting long-cold prefixes only.
